title: The Film That Opened to ₹1 Crore and Refused to Die: 'Main Vaapas Aaunga' Is 2026's Most Beautiful Sleeper Hit
excerpt: Diljit Dosanjh, A.R. Rahman, and Imtiaz Ali deliver a Partition love story that audiences are discovering by word of mouth — and it has quietly crossed ₹60 crore worldwide
body:
Here's a story Bollywood rarely gets to tell anymore.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=PRUTWluKRW8

Main Vaapas Aaunga opened on June 12 to the kind of numbers that make producers wince — ₹1.15 crore on day one, a polite 12% occupancy across 2,302 screens, and a weekend total that had trade analysts already writing the obituary. Imtiaz Ali's Partition-era love story, starring Diljit Dosanjh, Sharvari, Vedang Raina, and the incomparable Naseeruddin Shah, looked like it was headed for that most familiar of Bollywood fates: great reviews, empty theatres.

Then something happened. People who watched it wouldn't shut up about it.

The word started spreading the way it used to before algorithms decided everything — friends calling friends, Instagram stories with tear-streaked selfies, tweets about a particular A.R. Rahman track that wouldn't leave anyone's head. By the second weekend, the film had pulled off the rarest box office magic trick of all: day 11 through 14 earned more than day 1 through 7. That almost never happens. When it does, you know a film has touched something real.

> "As of two weeks in, Main Vaapas Aaunga has crossed ₹60 crore worldwide — a figure that seemed ludicrous when it was struggling to cross ₹8 crore in its first four days."

As of two weeks in, Main Vaapas Aaunga has crossed ₹60 crore worldwide — a figure that seemed ludicrous when it was struggling to cross ₹8 crore in its first four days. With a ₹70-crore budget, it's within striking distance of becoming a genuine box office success, and trade analysts are now projecting a ₹75-crore-plus lifetime run.

The Film

At 167 minutes, this is not a film in a hurry — and that's exactly the point. Imtiaz Ali, directing his 10th feature in a 22-year career that includes *Jab We Met*, *Rockstar*, and *Tamasha*, tells a love story split across two timelines and two sides of the most painful line ever drawn on a map.

Diljit Dosanjh is extraordinary here. The man who tours sold-out stadiums and has one of the most joyful public personas in Indian entertainment goes somewhere entirely different — quieter, more vulnerable, more devastating. Opposite him, Sharvari continues her incredible 2026 run (she's also part of YRF's *Alpha*), while Vedang Raina brings a youthful intensity that anchors the younger timeline. And Naseeruddin Shah, at this point in his career, could make a phone book feel like poetry. Here, he's the emotional fulcrum around which the film's past and present rotate.

The cinematography, by Sylvester Fonseca, drenches the Partition sections in amber and dust, while the contemporary timeline breathes in cooler blues. It's the kind of visual storytelling that makes you want to freeze frames and hang them on a wall.

And then there's the music. A.R. Rahman and Imtiaz Ali together is already a loaded combination — *Rockstar*, *Highway*, *Tamasha* — but what they've done here might be their most restrained and haunting collaboration yet. The soundtrack has been climbing charts independently of the film's box office trajectory, with tracks living on loop playlists across the diaspora.

Why This Hits Different for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora, Main Vaapas Aaunga doesn't just tell a story — it touches a nerve. The film deals with the wounds of Partition: the uprooting, the loss of home, the idea that you can belong to two places and neither at once. These are themes that resonate deeply with anyone who's ever straddled two countries. Diljit himself has become a bridge figure for NRIs — culturally rooted yet globally present, traditional yet entirely modern. He doesn't play an NRI in this film, but the emotions he channels are ones the diaspora understands on a cellular level.

The film is still running in theatres — catch it on the big screen if you can, because Rahman's score deserves that sound system. An OTT window is likely within 6-8 weeks given Applause Entertainment's typical distribution deals, which means it could be streaming in the US, UK, and Canada before August ends.

In a month where Bollywood has thrown everything at the wall — massive action franchises, ensemble comedies, spy universes, zombie thrillers — the quietest film in the room is the one that's refusing to go away. Main Vaapas Aaunga is proof that when the writing is honest, the music is perfect, and the performances are real, audiences will find you.

They just might take their time. And honestly? That might be the most Imtiaz Ali thing about it.
